title: Numerology Period Cycles: Calculate All Three From Your Birth Date
excerpt: Calculate the three Period Cycles from your birth month, day and year. Follow two worked dates and see why reports can disagree about the transition ages.
image_prompt: THREE LIFE PERIODS, three antique gold calendar blocks labeled MONTH, DAY, YEAR on plum velvet.
content:
Calculate the month, day and year separately

If your chart lists three Period Cycles, start by reading your birth date in words. The month gives the first number, the day of the month gives the second, and the year gives the third. On October 24, 1986, for example, the three inputs are October, 24 and 1986. They become 1, 6 and 6. You can check those labels even if your report gives unfamiliar age ranges. The numbers and the ages are two separate calculations.

Period Cycles belong to a Western numerology tradition that assigns symbolic themes to the earlier, middle and later parts of a life. The sums are reproducible when you know the rules. The themes are beliefs, and the age ranges are conventions within those beliefs. A chart can supply a writing prompt. Your actual circumstances and choices supply the material for it.

This worksheet uses the component reduction taught in Hans Decoz’s first numerology workshop. The age examples below use the labeled rows in that workshop. If you are checking a particular report, write its publisher and version at the top of your notes so you can compare its rules directly.

Three rows you can fill in on paper

  1. First Period, birth month. January through September already give 1 through 9. October gives 10, then 1. November gives 11, which this convention keeps. December gives 12, then 3. Use the position of the month in the calendar.
  2. Second Period, day of the month. Start with the actual calendar day. A day like 24 gives 2 + 4 = 6. Keep 11 and 22 when you reach them under this rule. The 29th gives 2 + 9 = 11, so 29 and 11 can give the same Second Period.
  3. Third Period, birth year. Add the four year digits and repeat as needed. For 1986 the trail is 1 + 9 + 8 + 6 = 24, then 2 + 4 = 6. Keep a supported master number when it appears. In the worked cases below, the only such stops are 11 and 22.

Write the original input next to the result. A line saying “day 29 → 11” is easier to audit than a bare 11. Use a fresh line for the year, even if you immediately recognize the same result as the day. The repetition is useful information about the calculation. If you found the input on a form that says 04/07, confirm whether it means April 7 or July 4 before starting. Interchanging those dates reverses the first two labels.

Some reports print 11/2 alongside a master-number result. In that notation 11 is the retained value and 2 is the single-digit reduction of the same number. Keep both in your notes if your report shows both. Our worked master-number guide shows how stop points can change what you record. Check the report’s rules for the particular row you are comparing, especially if you encounter a result such as 33.

Example one: October 24, 1986

PeriodBirth-date partArithmeticLabel
FirstOctober10 → 1 + 01
Second242 + 46
Third19861 + 9 + 8 + 6 = 24 → 2 + 46

To get the Life Path for the workshop’s timing lookup, add the three results: 1 + 6 + 6 = 13, then 1 + 3 = 4. Look up the row for 4. It shows 32/33 and 59/60. As an age-band shorthand, write First Period through age 32, Second Period at ages 33 through 59, and Third Period from age 60. The paired values in this table indicate adjacent ages around a changeover. They use a different notation from “11/2,” where the slash joins two representations of a number.

At age 45 this example sits in the second band with a label of 6. At age 65 it sits in the third band, also with a label of 6. If your notes only say “6,” somebody reading them later cannot tell which part of the birth date you used. Record “Second Period 6, from day 24” or “Third Period 6, from year 1986.” A repeated label is a normal result of reducing different inputs. You still have three rows and two changeovers.

One way to use that repetition as a prompt is to look at the same theme in two settings. Suppose you associate 6 with taking responsibility. For the middle years, you might recall the first responsibility you volunteered for and what made it worthwhile. For later years, you could ask which responsibilities you would like to share and with whom. You get two different questions from the same symbol, and you can answer both without assuming that the chart knows what your life will look like.

Example two: November 29, 1975

November is month 11. Day 29 gives 2 + 9 = 11. The year gives 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Under the retained-number convention these labels read 11, 11 and 22. A single-digit presentation would show 2, 2 and 4. The difference becomes easy to trace if you save the row where each number first appeared.

For the workshop timing lookup, 11 + 11 + 22 = 44 and 4 + 4 = 8. The Life Path 8 row reads 28/29 and 55/56. In everyday age bands, that is the First Period through age 28, the Second from 29 through 55 and the Third from 56 onward. A person with this fictional birth date would turn 29 in 2004 and 56 in 2031. Those years locate the birthdays for orientation. The workshop ties its transitions to a Personal Year convention, so the age row alone does not establish a date and time for a change.

Here is a quick diagnostic if the second result surprises you. If November appears as 2 while day 29 appears as 11, your source might use different stopping rules for months and days, or you may have copied one row from a report with a different convention. Check what the report actually says around each input. If all three entries are given as roots, you can reproduce 2, 2 and 4 with a consistent single-digit pass. In this example those roots happen to give the same Life Path 8. That agreement by itself tells you little about which rules the report used to display the Period labels.

When two reports show different ages

The age table deserves the same care as the arithmetic. Decoz’s Period Cycles reference treats timing as a Life Path lookup. The workshop gives a table and describes the start of the Second Period in terms of a nearby Personal Year 1. Numerologist.com’s Period Cycles worksheet instead describes the first boundary as approximately 36 minus the Life Path, with the middle period lasting 27 years. Its worked example prints age bands as inclusive ranges. Keep the label, the Life Path and the source’s boundary convention together when you take notes.

The difference shows up clearly with a Life Path 2. The Decoz workshop lists 25/26 and 52/53 for 2 and 11. Applying the other worksheet’s approximate formula to a plain 2 gives 36 − 2 = 34, and adding 27 gives 61. If two pages use those respective rules, a discrepancy of several years can arise even when the birth date and the three Period labels match. If a site displays a result without explaining its timing, you can verify the three labels first and leave its ages marked as unexplained.

Even when two tables agree, a line like “ends at 32” is ambiguous by itself. It might mean that 32 is the last age in the old band, or that the change happens around the birthday at which a person turns 32. Write out the last age of the old band and the first age of the new band whenever the source supplies both. For a journal entry about a transition, a broad window gives you room to describe what actually changed and how long it took.

How to tell Periods and Pinnacles apart on the same chart

Return to October 24, 1986 and put the numbers 1, 6 and 6 in front of you. The First Period is 1 because it uses the month alone. The First Pinnacle is 1 + 6 = 7 because its formula combines the month and day. In this example, the corresponding first age bands can look similar on reports, even though 1 and 7 are answers to different calculations. A practical clue is the number of entries: three in the Period row and four in the Pinnacle row.

Try checking the second entry as well. The Second Period equals day 24 reduced to 6. The Second Pinnacle combines the day and year results, so 6 + 6 = 12, then 1 + 2 = 3. When two sources disagree, ask “which row am I looking at?” before trying to reconcile the figures. The NumGuru Pinnacle worksheet walks through the four additions and its own age convention. Use its arithmetic to identify Pinnacle numbers and cite the timing table appropriate to the Period method you chose.

A Personal Year also answers a different question. It requires a target year, such as 2026. The Third Period uses the year of birth and can be calculated before you know which year you want to review. For a side-by-side check, keep the birth year fixed and change the target year in the Personal Year worksheet. The Personal Year calculation updates while all three Period labels stay in the same order. See the Personal Year start-date comparison when the question is which year applies around a birthday.

Use the worksheet for reflection

Give each row one question you could answer using actual experiences. For a First Period, ask what you learned from a setting you did not choose, such as your first school or the neighborhood where you grew up. For a Second Period, ask where your commitments have changed since you first took them on. For a Third Period, ask what you would enjoy passing on to somebody younger and how you might do it. Each question can be answered differently by people who share all three numbers.

You can also check a theme against two memories. Choose a situation where the word on the chart, such as “independence,” feels appropriate. Then pick another where that same word misses something important. Write a sentence about what each situation required. For example, repairing a chair alone might have been satisfying because you wanted practice. Asking a friend to help move a table might have been the sensible option because of the weight. The choice depended on the circumstances, and your notes can preserve that detail even when the same broad label covers both memories.

Keep birth dates and personal stories private if you are doing the worksheet with other people. You can compare the arithmetic by using the fictional dates above, or share just the numbered rows. If you want to compare the Life Path with your own broader chart, open the free NumGuru calculator on the homepage. Keep your Period worksheet beside it so you can identify which figures came from which calculation.

Three final checks before you file the worksheet

Check the inputs. Write the month in words, the day as a calendar day and the year as four digits. If you move the same birth date into another worksheet, copy those exact inputs. A date that crosses midnight in different time zones is a matter of which civil birth date you choose; record whichever date you used.

Check the three labels. Underline the first number at which each row stops, then copy those underlined values in order. If a report replaces a master number with a root, keep both forms and name the rule. When any two labels match, look at the underlying inputs before assuming you copied a line twice.

Check the age source. Record the Life Path, the title of the table or formula and the two age boundaries. If the table appears to disagree with the report, check how the report handles the last age of a band. Leave the age blank when a source does not explain its convention. The month, day and year calculations still give you three traceable labels to take to the next chart.
